citation.title: On the reliability of published findings using the regression discontinuity design in political science

standing_assumptions:
The article (Research and Politics, April–June 2023, pp. 1–12; printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers) is a survey and reanalysis of 45 published regression discontinuity (RD) studies. It states no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof and displays no formula; its mathematical content is in running text, in Tables 1–3 and in Figures 1–5. Every passage of the article quoted in this file was read from the page images. The official online supplement (Sections S1–S9, 23 pp.) is staged only as a text extraction, with no rendered pages; the few supplement passages quoted here (Section S4, Section S9, Figure S9) are transcribed from that extraction and are marked as such wherever they occur.
(S1) Estimand and identification. p. 3 (PDF p. 3), section ‘Why is it hard to estimate RD effects?’: “The causal effect studied in the RD design is the difference between the expected treated and control potential outcomes at a cutoff where treatment assignment changes in a discontinuous fashion. If the conditional expectation function of the outcome were known, this effect can be calculated without error under an assumption that the conditional expectation functions of the potential outcomes are continuous at the cut point. In other words, the RD effect is identified under a continuity assumption.” The paper uses no symbols for these objects. The targets write $X$ for the running variable, $c$ for the cutoff, $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ for the potential outcomes, $D = \mathbf{1}\{X \ge c\}$ for treatment in a sharp design, and $\tau = E[Y(1)\mid X = c] - E[Y(0)\mid X = c]$ for the RD effect, with both conditional expectation functions continuous at $c$.
(S2) Estimation. p. 3 (PDF p. 3): “The standard way to proceed is to assume that the potential outcome functions are smooth, meaning that they do not change too quickly. This implies that observations close to the cutoff are somewhat informative of the value of the functions at the cutoff, so they can be used for estimation.” and “We can interpret this as a bias–variance trade-off, where the bias is governed by the relevance of the observations and the variance by their numbers.” No smoothness class, bound or rate is stated.
(S3) Inference. p. 3 (PDF p. 3): “To conduct hypothesis tests or construct confidence intervals, researchers need to estimate the accuracy of the RD point estimate. Conventional methods used to gauge this accuracy rely on an assumption that the bias of the estimator is negligible compared to its variance, as would be the case in, for example, a randomized experiment. However, when a bandwidth selection method balances bias and variance to maximize accuracy, the bias is not negligible, and it must therefore be accounted for when drawing inference. Researchers sometimes neglect doing so, with the consequence that their hypothesis tests and confidence intervals are misleading even when the sample is large.” The three remedies the paper recognizes, pp. 3–4 (PDF pp. 3–4): “The first approach is so-called undersmoothing, meaning that one uses a bandwidth that is smaller than the optimal one. If done correctly, this will ensure that the bias indeed is negligible in large samples, so researchers can use conventional methods to construct hypothesis tests and confidence intervals.”; “The second approach is to adjust the inference procedure for the bias. […] The alternative approach described by Calonico et al. (2014), which is becoming the standard approach used in political science, is to also estimate the precision of the bias adjustment and incorporate this into the variance estimator. This allows researchers to use bias adjustments that have similar precision as the point estimator (e.g., as would be the case when the same bandwidth is used for both point and bias estimation), and it should improve finite sample performance.”; “The third approach is to adjust the inference procedure with the worse-case bias consistent with the observed data. The worst-case is taken with respect to a stipulated class of functions, in which the true conditional expectation function is assumed to exist.”
(S4) Sample and $t$-statistics. p. 4 (PDF p. 4): “There were 45 studies in total that satisfied these inclusion criteria.” and “Figure 1 presents the distribution of $t$-statistics for the published findings among all 45 studies in our sample. The first panel presents the distribution of the main reported result of each article, meaning that each article contributes one $t$-statistic. The second panel presents the distribution of all results that were referenced in the articles’ abstracts, which we take as a proxy for being a primary result of an article. There are 80 $t$-statistics in total in the second panel, meaning that each article contributes 1.78 statistics on average. To avoid overrepresentation of articles that present many results, the $t$-statistics in the second panel are weighted by the inverse of the total number of results in each study. For the majority of the studies, we either use reported $t$-statistics or reconstruct $t$-statistics using the ratio of coefficients and standard errors. For the small number of the studies where neither $t$-statistics nor standard errors were reported, we reconstruct $t$-statistics using reported $p$-values, confidence intervals and point estimates, or using replication code and data provided by the authors.” The horizontal axis of the histograms is labelled ‘t−statistic’, with ticks 0.98, 1.96, 2.94, 3.92; that the plotted and tested statistics are absolute values is read from the replication code, not from the text.
(S5) Reanalysis. p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Methodology: “We were able to obtain such data for 36 out of the 45 studies in our sample.”; “Our primary reanalysis uses the default settings in the R package rdrobust (Calonico et al., 2015). The procedure implemented in this package has well-understood theoretical properties and attempts to address the concerns discussed in the \emph{Why is it hard to estimate RD effects?} section. The reanalysis results we present in the main body of the paper exclude all studies that originally used the rdrobust package to estimate the effects, as a reanalysis would bring few new insights for these studies. This results in 39 estimates across 25 studies.”; “One limitation of the approach by Calonico et al. (2015) is that it is motivated by an asymptotic approximation. This means that confidence intervals and hypothesis tests may not be valid in finite samples.” The three panels of Figures 3 and 4 (p. 7, Results) are: the original analyses; “the default bandwidth selection method implemented in rdrobust (“mserd”)” with no “adjustments for bias for the point estimator nor any adjustments for the standard errors”; and the same bandwidth selection with “the bias adjustment for the point estimator” and estimated standard errors adjusted “to account for the added imprecision of the bias adjustment”.
(S6) Power analysis. p. 9 (PDF p. 9): “To investigate the extent to which this is a relevant concern among RD studies in political science, we conducted retrospective power analyses for all 36 studies with replication data, comprising 64 separate analyses. Using the power analysis method implemented in the R package rdpower by Cattaneo et al. (2019), we estimate the power of a two-tailed test at the 5% significance level based on a central limit approximation for the sampling distribution. The power analyses presume that $p$-values will be constructed with the bias adjustment and robust standard errors as implemented by rdrobust. As this procedure is only asymptotically valid, our power calculations may be optimistic relative to approaches that control the false positive rate in finite samples.”; “We measure effect size by Cohen’s $d$, which is the treatment effect standardized by the standard deviation of the outcome (Cohen, 1988). We use the standard deviation of the outcome of control units within the default bandwidth in the rdrobust package for this standardization. We investigate the effect sizes 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8.”; “Table 2 presents the results from the power analyses. The cells give the proportion of the 64 analyses that attain the power specified by the columns for the effect size specified by the rows. For example, we see that only 17% of the analyses attain 60% power to detect a standardized effect of 0.1. We weigh the analyses in the same way as in Figure 1(b) to account for the fact that some studies conducted more analyses than others.”
(S7) Notation of the targets that is not in the paper. $\Phi$ and $\varphi$ are the distribution function and density of $N(0,1)$. $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$ is the two-sided 5% normal critical value; the paper prints its rounding $1.96 = 49/25$ and the replication code uses the unrounded quantile ($1.95996398454000 < z < 1.95996398454010$). The normal-approximation power of the two-tailed 5% test of (S6), for a statistic distributed $N(\tau/s, 1)$ with $s > 0$, is $f(|\tau|/s)$ with $$f(a) = \Phi(a - z) + \Phi(-a - z), \qquad a \ge 0 .$$ For integers $0 \le k \le n$ and $p \in [0,1]$, $G_{n,k}(p) = \sum_{j=k}^{n} \binom{n}{j} p^j (1-p)^{n-j}$ is the upper tail of the Binomial$(n,p)$ distribution. Where a target takes a number from the deposited replication files (a stored standard error, a count, a weight), it says so and treats the number as a premise; such premises are not part of the mathematics to be proved.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: p. 7, the two sentences describing the standardization and the significance boundary of Figure 4, corrected: the divisor is the sample standard deviation and the boundary has slope 1/z, about 1/1.96
canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Results, right column, paragraph beginning ‘We can disaggregate the information in Figure 3’; Figure 4, p. 8 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; p. 7] “We use the sample variance of the outcome among control units for the standardization. The boundary for statistical significance at the 5% level is a line emanating from the origin with a slope of 1.96, here drawn in red, where estimates to the right of this line attain statistical significance at the conventional level.”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-E003), verbatim] “On page 7 replace 'sample variance' with 'sample standard deviation' and replace 'a slope of 1.96' with 'a slope of 1/z_{.975} approximately equal to 1/1.96'. Retain the statement that estimates to the right of the corrected line are significant at the conventional level.” [Corrected text; prior_correction.corrected_text, which Sol accepts as correct, verbatim] “We use the sample standard deviation of the outcome among control units for the standardization. The boundary for statistical significance at the 5% level is a line emanating from the origin with a slope of 1/z_{.975} approximately equal to 1/1.96, here drawn in red, where estimates to the right of this line attain statistical significance at the conventional level.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Coordinates $x = |\hat\beta|/s_0$ and $y = \mathrm{SE}/s_0$ with $s_0 > 0$ and $\mathrm{SE} > 0$; critical value $\zeta > 0$ (the paper's $1.96$; the code's $\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$).
(i) [The standardization cancels in the $t$-ratio] For real $\beta$ and nonzero $s$ and $\mathrm{SE}$: $\dfrac{\beta/s}{\mathrm{SE}/s} = \dfrac{\beta}{\mathrm{SE}}$. Hence $x/y = |\hat\beta|/\mathrm{SE} = |t|$ whatever the positive divisor.
(ii) [The boundary] For real $x$ and nonzero $y$ and $\zeta$: $x/y = \zeta \iff y = x/\zeta$. So the set of points with $|t| = \zeta$ is the line through the origin with slope $1/\zeta$ in the $(x, y)$ plane.
(iii) [The significant side] For $y > 0$ and $\zeta > 0$: $\zeta \le x/y \iff y \le x/\zeta \iff x \ge \zeta y$. So the estimates with $|t| \ge \zeta$ are those on or below the line $y = x/\zeta$, equivalently on or to the right of it at a given height, as the paper says of the line it draws.
(iv) [The constant] $1/\tfrac{49}{25} = \tfrac{25}{49}$ and $\tfrac{25}{49} < 1 < \tfrac{49}{25}$: the slope is the reciprocal of the printed value, about $0.5102$. With $\zeta = \Phi^{-1}(0.975)$ the slope is $0.51021\ldots$; the difference from $\tfrac{25}{49} = 0.51020\ldots$ is the rounding of $1.96$.
(v) [The divisor] The standardizing quantity is the sample standard deviation $s_0 = \sqrt{v}$ of the control outcomes, where $v$ is their sample variance; $\sqrt v = v$ only if $v \in \{0, 1\}$. For $n$ binary outcomes with $k$ ones ($n \ge 2$), $v = \dfrac{k(n-k)}{n(n-1)}$. Source check (premise from the deposited data): for Boas and Hidalgo (2011) the control outcomes are $82$ ones and $486$ zeros, so $v = \tfrac{82 \cdot 486}{568 \cdot 567} = \tfrac{123}{994}$, and the stored standardizing value $\delta = 0.351770457441169$ satisfies $(\delta - 10^{-14})^2 < \tfrac{123}{994} < (\delta + 10^{-14})^2$: it is $\sqrt{123/994}$, not $\tfrac{123}{994} = 0.1237\ldots$
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. p. 7 (PDF p. 7): “We can disaggregate the information in Figure 3 using a funnel plot, which is a scatter plot with standardized point estimates and standardized estimated standard errors on the two axes. Figure 4 presents such a funnel plot for the 39 estimates in the replication study.$^{3}$ We use the sample variance of the outcome among control units for the standardization. The boundary for statistical significance at the 5% level is a line emanating from the origin with a slope of 1.96, here drawn in red, where estimates to the right of this line attain statistical significance at the conventional level.” Figure 4, p. 8 (PDF p. 8): in each panel the horizontal axis is labelled ‘Point estimate’ (ticks 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0), the vertical axis ‘Standard error’ (ticks 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), and the red line through the origin is labelled ‘t = 1.96’. p. 8: “We note that the estimates cluster around the red line corresponding to a $t$-statistic of 1.96, especially in the first panel.”
Not in the paper (read by the validator from the deposited plotting script): the plotted coordinates are $x = |\hat\beta|/s_0$ and $y = \mathrm{SE}/s_0$, where $s_0$ is the sample standard deviation of the outcome among observations below the cutoff, and the red line is drawn with slope $1/\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$. The $t$-statistic of a plotted estimate is $|t| = |\hat\beta|/\mathrm{SE}$; ‘slope’ means the coefficient $k$ in the equation $y = kx$ of the line in the plotted coordinates.
canonical_claim.note: Priority 3 (Minor). The repair costs nothing: two words change, and the figure, the code and every number stand. (i)–(iii) are the validator's Lean theorems `standardized_ratio`, `significance_boundary` and `significance_side`, and (iv) is `reciprocal_slope` (runs/P033/validate/P033-E003/v1/artifact/check.lean); (v) is section 2 of the validator's derivation.md. In (iii) the paper's ‘to the right of this line’ is correct for the line actually drawn; only its stated slope is wrong. The standardization of the power analysis on p. 9 (standard deviation within the bandwidth) is a separate, correctly described quantity. The inequality in (v) was rechecked for this list with exact rational arithmetic.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Figure S9 (vertical axis ‘RDHonest P−Value’, caption ‘Original p-values vs. p-values derived using RDHonest’), with the pseudo t-statistics of p. 8 of the main text: the normal-tail transform of a 95% bias-aware interval, read as a p-value; the witness is the validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: Supplement, Figure S9 (printed supplement p. 18) and Section S9 (printed supplement p. 16), text extraction only; main text p. 8 (PDF p. 8), right column, top paragraph
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact counterexample (the validator's construction; not in the paper): a Gaussian model with a known bound on the bias in which the 95% bias-aware interval is exactly honest and the transform $p_*$ of that interval rejects a true null with probability above $\tfrac15$ at nominal level $\tfrac15$. Model and notation as in definitions_needed, with $B = 1$.
(i) [The interval] There is a unique $H > 0$ with $\Phi(H - 1) - \Phi(-H - 1) = \tfrac{19}{20}$, and $2.64614554821530 < H < 2.64614554821540$.
(ii) [It is exactly honest] For every $\theta$ and every $|b| \le 1$, $P_{\theta, b}\big(\theta \in [T - H, T + H]\big) = \Phi(H - b) - \Phi(-H - b) \ge \tfrac{19}{20}$, with equality if and only if $|b| = 1$.
(iii) [The transform] $p_*(T) = 2\Phi(-z|T|/H)$ with $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$, $1.95996398454000 < z < 1.95996398454010$: the paper's conversion applied to the estimate $T$ and the half-length $H$.
(iv) [It over-rejects at level one fifth] Let $q = \Phi^{-1}(9/10)$ ($1.28155156554460 < q < 1.28155156554470$) and $C = Hq/z$ ($1.73022157382648 < C < 1.73022157382677$). Then $\{p_* \le \tfrac15\} = \{|T| \ge C\}$, and at $\theta = 0$, $b = 1$, $$P_{0,1}\big(p_* \le \tfrac15\big) = \Phi(1 - C) + \Phi(-1 - C), \qquad 0.23579196727091 < P_{0,1}\big(p_* \le \tfrac15\big) < 0.23579196727101,$$ which exceeds $\tfrac15$.
(v) [A smaller bias bound also fails] With $B = b = \tfrac12$ and $H$ the unique positive root of $\Phi(H - \tfrac12) - \Phi(-H - \tfrac12) = \tfrac{19}{20}$ ($2.18147744232810 < H < 2.18147744232820$): $0.20414905632765 < P_{0,1/2}(p_* \le \tfrac15) < 0.20414905632774$, again above $\tfrac15$.
Conclusion. $p_*$ is not a valid $p$-value for the null $\theta = 0$ in this model, although its input interval has worst-case coverage exactly $\tfrac{19}{20}$: the defining inequality fails at $\alpha = \tfrac15$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper, main text, p. 8 (PDF p. 8), read from the page image: “Because the rdhonest package uses a worst-case bias adjustment, conventional t-statistics will not capture the adjustment made here. To make the results from rdhonest comparable to the other results in this paper, we derive pseudo $t$-statistics based on the width of the confidence intervals produced by the rdhonest package. Substantively, the distribution of reanalysis results is similar to those produced by rdrobust: the pseudo $t$-statistics shift to the left, and the pseudo standard errors systematically increase.” The worst-case approach, p. 4: quoted in (S3).
From the supplement, text extraction only (no rendered page is staged; the validator also rendered the replication package's own Figure S9 PDF, which shows the same labels). Section S9 (printed supplement p. 16): “We construct pseudo t-statistics for the rdhonest package using the length of the confidence interval that include the bias adjustment.” Figure S9 (printed supplement p. 18): horizontal axis “Original P−Value”; vertical axis “RDHonest P−Value”; title “Original versus RDHonest P−Value”; subtitle “(Studies with Replication Data Reanalyzed with RDHonest)”; caption “Figure S9: Original p-values vs. p-values derived using RDHonest”.
Not in the paper (read by the validator from the deposited script run-reanalysis.R): with $\hat\theta$ the RDHonest estimate and $h > 0$ the half-length of its reported 95% bias-aware interval $[\hat\theta - h, \hat\theta + h]$, the plotted quantity is $$\tilde s = h/z, \qquad \tilde t = |\hat\theta|/\tilde s, \qquad p_* = 2\Phi(-\tilde t) = 2\Phi\big(-z|\hat\theta|/h\big), \qquad z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40).$$ [$p$-value] A statistic $P$ is a valid $p$-value for a null hypothesis if $P_0(P \le \alpha) \le \alpha$ for every $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and every distribution $P_0$ in the null. [The Gaussian bias-aware model of the validator] $T = \theta + b + Z$ with $Z \sim N(0,1)$; $\theta$ is the parameter of interest and $b$ an unknown bias with $|b| \le B$, $B \ge 0$ known; the null $\theta = 0$ is the family $\{N(b, 1) : |b| \le B\}$; $P_{\theta, b}$ denotes probability under $(\theta, b)$.
canonical_claim.note: P033-E001 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json; second rating borderline error/clarity note). The label is in a supplementary figure whose rendered page is not staged: the labels and caption are transcribed from the supplement's text extraction and agree with the replication package's Figure S9 PDF, which the validator rendered. The main text calls the underlying quantities pseudo $t$-statistics. Sol's verdict is confirmed (upheld on re-run), evidence type exact counterexample. Not established, and not asserted: a false-positive rate for any of the 46 plotted estimates, or failure at every level other than 5%. Source: sections 2–4 of the validator's derivation.md; exact_counterexample.py certifies every enclosure with rational arithmetic (Machin's formula for $\pi$, alternating Taylor bounds for $\Phi$). The enclosures were recomputed for this list at 40 digits: $H = 2.6461455482153111\ldots$, $C = 1.7302215738265288\ldots$, probability $0.2357919672709916\ldots$; second model $H = 2.1814774423281543\ldots$, probability $0.2041490563277117\ldots$ For a proof of ‘$> \tfrac15$’ cruder bounds suffice. The finding relates to the RDHonest part of P033-H4.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Figure S9, corrected: the vertical quantity is a pseudo p-value, the normal-tail transform of the pseudo t-statistic of p. 8; it reproduces the 5% decision of the 95% interval and is not in general a valid p-value at other levels
canonical_claim.location: Supplement, Figure S9 (printed supplement p. 18), text extraction only; main text p. 8 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; Supplement Figure S9, from the text extraction] Vertical axis: “RDHonest P−Value”. Title: “Original versus RDHonest P−Value”. Caption: “Figure S9: Original p-values vs. p-values derived using RDHonest”. [Printed; main text, p. 8, from the page image] “To make the results from rdhonest comparable to the other results in this paper, we derive pseudo $t$-statistics based on the width of the confidence intervals produced by the rdhonest package.”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-E001), verbatim] “Retain the numbers, label the vertical axis 'RDHonest pseudo p-value', and change the title/caption to identify normal-tail transforms of interval-based pseudo t-statistics. Give the formula and state that p_star<0.05 is equivalent to the reported 95% interval excluding zero, with any 5% validity inherited from the interval's assumptions. State that the transforms are not generally valid p-values at other levels.” [Corrected text; prior_correction.corrected_text, verbatim] “Figure S9: Original p-values versus normal-tail transforms of RDHonest pseudo t-statistics. The vertical quantity is p_star = 2 Phi(-z_0.975 |estimate|/h), where h is the reported 95% bias-aware confidence-interval half-length. The rule p_star<0.05 is exactly equivalent to this interval excluding zero. These transforms are not generally valid p-values at other significance levels; any 5% validity inherits the interval's coverage assumptions. Vertical-axis label: RDHonest pseudo p-value. Title: Original p-values versus RDHonest pseudo p-values.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$; for a real estimate $\hat\theta$ and a half-length $h > 0$, $\tilde s = h/z$, $\tilde t = |\hat\theta|/\tilde s$ and $p_* = 2\Phi(-\tilde t) = 2\Phi(-z|\hat\theta|/h)$.
(i) [The 5% decision is that of the interval] $p_* < \tfrac{1}{20} \iff |\hat\theta| > h \iff 0 \notin [\hat\theta - h, \hat\theta + h]$, and $p_* \le \tfrac{1}{20} \iff |\hat\theta| \ge h$. This is algebra and needs no sampling assumption.
(ii) [Its size at 5% is inherited from the interval] In the Gaussian bias-aware model of definitions_needed, with $B \ge 0$ and $H$ the unique positive root of $\Phi(H - B) - \Phi(-H - B) = \tfrac{19}{20}$, and $p_*(T) = 2\Phi(-z|T|/H)$: for every $|b| \le B$, $P_{0,b}\big(p_* < \tfrac{1}{20}\big) = 1 - \big[\Phi(H - b) - \Phi(-H - b)\big] \le \tfrac{1}{20}$, with equality if and only if $|b| = B$.
(iii) [Without bias it is the ordinary $p$-value] If $B = 0$, then $H = z$, $p_*(T) = 2\Phi(-|T|)$, and $P_{0,0}(p_* \le \alpha) = \alpha$ for every $\alpha \in (0,1)$.
(iv) [Not valid at other levels in general] For $B = 1$, $P_{0,1}(p_* \le \tfrac15) > \tfrac15$ (P033-T12).
(v) [A valid $p$-value in the same model] For $B \ge 0$ let $p_B(t) = \Phi(B - |t|) + \Phi(-B - |t|)$. Then $p_B(0) = 1$, $p_B$ is continuous and strictly decreasing in $|t|$ with limit $0$, and for every $|b| \le B$ and every $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $$P_{0,b}\big(p_B(T) \le \alpha\big) \le \alpha, \quad\text{with equality when } |b| = B ;$$ moreover $p_B(T) \le \tfrac{1}{20} \iff |T| \ge H \iff p_*(T) \le \tfrac{1}{20}$, so $p_B$ and $p_*$ make the same decision at the 5% level.

canonical_claim.note: Priority 3 (Minor). The repair relabels the figure and keeps every plotted number, interval and 5% decision. (i) is section 1, (ii)–(iv) sections 2–3 and (v) section 5 of the validator's derivation.md. (ii) and (v) are statements about the fixed-variance, fixed-bound Gaussian model; they do not say that the paper's intervals, whose smoothness bound is estimated from the data (p. 7), have exact 95% coverage, and (v) is not offered as a replacement for the published figure (‘It does not authorize plugging in an arbitrary estimated B or s’). In (v) the model has variance 1; the validator states it for a known variance $s^2$ with $p_B(t) = \Phi((B - |t|)/s) + \Phi((-B - |t|)/s)$. The premise that all 46 plotted values equal $p_*$ computed from the stored intervals is read from the deposited results and is not part of the formal statement.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Section S4: standard errors imputed from ‘the upper value of the reported … confidence interval’ and the point estimate (Ariga; Holbein; Klašnja and Titiunik), with the main-text sentence of p. 4, against the rule that produced the published statistics; the witnesses are rows of the deposited metadata and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: Supplement, Section S4 (printed supplement pp. 9–10), text extraction only; main text p. 4 (PDF p. 4), right column, end of the paragraph on Figure 1
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witnesses (the validator's calculation on recorded values; not in the paper) that the rule described in Supplement S4 and the rule that produced the published statistics are different functions of the reported numbers. Notation $s_U$, $s_W$ as in definitions_needed. [The recorded estimates and intervals, and the fact that the published statistics follow $s_W$, are premises read from the deposited metadata and code.]
(i) [Klašnja and Titiunik (2017)] Recorded: $\beta = -\tfrac{3}{20}$, $L = -\tfrac{213}{1000}$, $U = -\tfrac{101}{1000}$. canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; Supplement S4, from the text extraction] Ariga (2015) (a-b): “The standard error estimate was imputed by (a) subtracting the point estimate value from the upper value of the reported 90% confidence interval, and then (b) dividing that value by the critical value for a 90% confidence interval (1.64).” Holbein (2016) (a-c), and in the same words the entry for Klašnja and Titiunik (2017): “The standard error was not explicitly listed and so we imputed by using the upper bound of a 95% CI and the point estimate along with the critical value of 1.96.” [Printed; main text, p. 4, from the page image] “For the small number of the studies where neither $t$-statistics nor standard errors were reported, we reconstruct $t$-statistics using reported $p$-values, confidence intervals and point estimates, or using replication code and data provided by the authors.”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-N003), verbatim] “Align the account with the reproduced code: remove 'reported p-values' from the main-text list of t-statistic reconstruction sources; describe interval SEs in S4 as the full interval width divided by twice Phi^{-1}(0.95) for 90% intervals and twice Phi^{-1}(0.975) for 95% intervals; clarify that reported p-values are recorded separately and missing p-values derived by normal approximation. Update the Klasnja-Titiunik raw metadata note to describe width. Leave the released calculations unchanged.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] $\beta$ real, $L < U$, $q > 0$; $s_U = (U - \beta)/q$ and $s_W = (U - L)/(2q)$.
(i) [The corrected rule] For a reported interval $[L, U]$ of nominal level $1 - \alpha$, the imputed standard error is $s_W = \dfrac{U - L}{2\,q_\alpha}$ with $q_\alpha = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)$, that is $q = \Phi^{-1}(0.95)$ for a 90% interval and $q = \Phi^{-1}(0.975)$ for a 95% interval; the reconstructed statistic is $|t| = |\beta|/s_W$, and a missing $p$-value is $2\Phi(-|t|)$. The point estimate does not enter $s_W$.
(ii) [When the two rules agree] $2q\,(s_W - s_U) = 2\beta - (L + U)$. Hence $s_W = s_U$ if and only if $\beta = \tfrac{L + U}{2}$, $s_W > s_U$ if and only if $\beta > \tfrac{L+U}{2}$, and $s_W < s_U$ if and only if $\beta < \tfrac{L+U}{2}$.
(iii) [Both recover the standard error of an exact normal interval] If $L = \beta - q s$ and $U = \beta + q s$ for some $s > 0$, then $s_W = s_U = s$.
(iv) [The recorded Klašnja and Titiunik row under the corrected rule] With $\beta = -\tfrac{3}{20}$, $L = -\tfrac{213}{1000}$, $U = -\tfrac{101}{1000}$: $s_W = \tfrac{7}{125\,q}$ and $|t_W| = \tfrac{75\,q}{28}$; at $q = \tfrac{49}{25}$ these are $\tfrac{1}{35}$ and $\tfrac{21}{4}$.
